title: National segmentation
text: A national segmentation layer was created to provide the spatial unit of assessment for the BII land use and intensity layers. Regular grid cells may impose artificial boundaries on the landscape and frequently contain mixtures of land uses, particularly in heterogeneous landscapes, which can obscure the ecological meaning of assigned classes. In contrast, segmentation tools provide an approach for extracting features from satellite imagery based on objects, potentially grouping pixels into spatially contiguous units based on similarity, producing units that more closely align with underlying vegetation structure, land use patterns, and management units. The objects can then be grouped into classes that represent real-world features. BII land use classes are intended to represent landscape-scale land use contexts linked to species responses, rather than individual pixels. Defining analysis units that better reflect real-world landscape “organisation” therefore improves the ecological interpretability of land use classification and provides a more appropriate basis for assigning land use intensity and estimating biodiversity intactness.

title: National segmentation
text:
Parameter selection and analysis
Segmentation was implemented in Google Earth Engine using the Simple Non-Iterative Clustering algorithm (SNIC,or superpixel clustering) applied to the AlphaEarth Foundations Embeddings (Brown et al., 2025). The embeddings provide a condensed representation of landscape characteristics derived from multiple sensors and environmental variables, including optical reflectance (e.g. Sentinel-2, Landsat 8 & 9), radar backscatter (e.g. Sentinel-1, PALSAR-2 and GEDI), climate (e.g. ERA5-Land), land cover context (NLCD), and topographic (GLO-30 DEM) information. Rather than representing a single spectral index or satellite band, each embedding dimension, of which there are 64, captures complex spatial, spectral and temporal patterns learned from large volumes of EO data.  So, instead of asking do these pixels have similar spectral values, it asks do these pixels have similar embedding signatures or landscape “fingerprints” (vegetation, soil, topography etc.)?
The key parameter: “size” controls how large each segment is, with smaller values producing numerous small, detailed segments and larger values producing fewer, larger segments that represent broader landscape units. The “compactness” parameter controls whether segments follow natural patterns in the data (low values, more irregular and realistic shapes) or form more regular, uniform shapes (high values). This was set to 1 to allow segments to follow natural landscape boundaries while maintaining some spatial regularity.”Connectivity” controls how pixels are considered connected, where 8 allows diagonal connections (on top of the 4 direct neighbours) and results in smoother, more continuous segments. We tested three sizes: fine (size = 15; c. 150 m), medium (size = 40; c. 400 m), and coarse (size = 100; c. 1 km), to evaluate how segment size influences the representation of landscape heterogeneity and land-use systems. Smaller segments captured fine-scale variation such as field boundaries and patchy vegetation but over-fragmented the landscape (e.g. detect small mosaiced plant communities within a wetland), whereas larger segments represented broader land-use systems but merged some distinct land uses (different crops). An intermediate scale (800m) was selected for further analysis as it best balanced ecological realism and spatial coherence. The neighbourhood size was scaled proportionally to segment size (size × 4) to ensure stable region growth and minimise edge artefacts. Projection and scale were fixed before segmentation to reduce zoom-dependent behaviour in GEE visualisation and to improve reproducibility of the exported outputs.
The segmentation was generated once for the national extent and saved as a reusable asset. The same segment identifiers are used for all subsequent land use proportion and intensity calculations.

title: South African BII land use intensity workflow
text: This page documents the progress toward creating a national Biodiversity Intactness Index for South Africa. It highlights current status in the land use intensity analysis workflow, describes potential next steps and decisions that still require discussion. At the top of each page we show what still needs to be done.

title: South African BII land use intensity workflow
text: This page documents the progress toward creating a national Biodiversity Intactness Index for South Africa. It highlights current status in the land use intensity analysis workflow, describes potential next steps and decisions that still require discussion. At the top of each page we show what still needs to be done.

title: South African BII land use intensity workflow
text:
Workflow summary
This workflow combines the South African National Land Cover (NLC) 2022, the South African National Protected Area Database (SAPAD) and biome-specific ecocsystem condition data to produce segment-based land use and land use intensity layers to develop a South African Biodiversity Intactness Index.
The unit of assessment is a spatial segment rather than an individual raster pixel. At the end of the workflow, each segment receives:

one dominant BII land use class; and
one land use intensity estimate between 0 and 1.

The pages are split into four sections:

National segmentation
National land use reclassification
National segment land use and intensity allocation
Context-specific land use intensity score refinement of “untransformed”

title: South African BII land use intensity workflow
text:
Current status
The worflow is setup as three GEE scripts, with data saved as GEE assets and can be updated iteratively.

Step 1: National segmentation tested and completed.
Step 2: NLC reclassification steps completed

NLC classes crosswalked to BII broad land use classes
SAPAD appropriate BII classes selected and cleaned

Step 3: Calculate proportions of broad land use classes within each segment completed
Step 4 : Assign dominant land use class using sequential decision tree first iteration completed
Step 5: Assign intensity for BII land use classes 1-4 from NLC first iteration completed
Step 6: Assign intensity for BII land use class 6 (untransformed). In progress



Provisional 6 step workflow for generation of a land use intensity layer for South Africa

title: South African BII land use intensity workflow
text:
Next steps

Different datasets are now being tested as an additional source of intensity information.
Explore detection of low intensity SANLC classes

title: Land use intensity
text:
Land cover classification inevitably contains uncertainty because different land uses can have similar spectral signatures, individual pixels can contain mixtures of vegetation and built surfaces, and seasonal changes can alter their appearance. Categories such as smallholdings, villages and urban recreational land are particularly difficult to distinguish because their defining differences involve land use and management, which are not always observable from satellite imagery. Correcting these errors nationally would require additional reference data and substantial reclassification, beyond the scope of this BII component. We therefore need an intensity approach that is robust to uncertainty in the underlying map.
Confusion among subclasses belonging to the same broad land use leaves broad allocation unchanged, but can affect intensity estimates if those subclasses receive different scores. We are consequently comparing SANLC-based scores with additional data sources as indicators of land use pressure. These comparisons are exploratory; the final approach has not yet been selected.
In particular the land cover classes that fall within the “low intensity” gradient, might fit according to the class description, but in reality the classifier struggles to discern these and it is where much of the SANLC misclassification occurs.

Linking intensity to the expert assessments
The BII experts estimated the abundance remaining for each species group under specified landscape scenarios, relative to an intact reference. For four broad land uses, paired scenarios define the endpoints of an intensity gradient. Spatial intensity scores determine how the corresponding expert intactness estimates are interpolated.
FOr the sub-Saharan African BII, relevant proxies were standardised to 0–1, averaged with equal weights, and the resulting average intensity rescaled within each broad land-use class. These are relative intensity scores, rather than direct measurements of biodiversity loss.
Because there is such a detailed 73 class land cover classification available in South Africa, our “SANLC alternative approach” assigns provisional scores of 0, 0.5 and 1 to detailed subclasses and calculates their area-weighted mean within the assigned land-cover class in each segment. Where there is still uncertainty in subclass classification (i.e. where land cover is often misclassified), additional spatial data may be needed to estimate land use intensity.


Settlements
Endpoints: mixed settlements → dense urban.
Sub-Saharan BII: Settlement intensity combined mapped settlement extent from World Settlement Footprint with mean population density across each grid cell. These represented the transition from dispersed development interspersed with gardens and open vegetation to densely developed landscapes.
South African approach: We are comparing this method with scores assigned to SANLC residential, village, smallholding, recreational, industrial and mining subclasses. Additional footprint and population information may reduce dependence on uncertain subclass distinctions.


Timber plantations
Single scenario: timber plantations.
Sub-Saharan BII: No variable intensity gradient was calculated. Experts assessed one plantation scenario encompassing timber production, harvesting and replanting, with some remnant natural vegetation.
South African approach: We currently retain a single category. SANLC distinguishes standing, sparse and clear-felled plantations, but these may represent stages of the same rotation rather than distinct management intensities. Using these differences to adjust BII would require an additional ecological basis.


Tree croplands
Endpoints: non-intensive smallholder croplands → tree-crop plantations.
Sub-Saharan BII: Intensity combined tree-crop coverage, field-size scores and nitrogen fertiliser inputs. The smallholder scenario served as the low-intensity endpoint because these landscapes can contain both annual crops and useful trees; the other endpoint represented tree-crop plantations, including orchards and vineyards.
South African approach: Both SANLC orchards and vines currently receive a high score, so their within-class average provides no intensity gradient. We are testing whether tree-crop coverage, field size and agricultural-input data provide meaningful differentiation. Their usefulness will depend on their spatial detail and relevance to South African production systems.


Croplands
Endpoints: non-intensive smallholder croplands → intensive large-scale croplands.
Sub-Saharan BII: Intensity combined crop coverage, field-size scores and nitrogen fertiliser inputs. Together, these represented differences in landscape composition, agricultural scale and input intensity.
South African approach: The SANLC commercial temporary and permanent cropland subclasses correspond well to the intensive large scale croplands the intensive large-scale croplands end poitn, i.e. a score of 1. But the small-scale annual crops, which from the description of the class seems ideal for the low end point here, often have the same land use intensity signals as the commercial crops. We’ve given it a score of 0.5 for this comparison stage. We are comparing these scores with the proxy-based method and considering whether SANLC distinctions such as irrigation can provide further useful information.


Protected lands
Single scenario: strictly protected areas.
Sub-Saharan BII: No variable intensity gradient was calculated. The expert scenario described restricted settlement and resource use, limited recent human impacts, and some tourism infrastructure.
South African approach: Protected-area coverage informs allocation, with priority above untransformed land. We retain underlying SANLC composition for assessment, but do not currently assign an intensity gradient. Legal protection does not necessarily imply effective management or intact ecological condition; accounting for those differences would require additional evidence.


Untransformed lands
Endpoints: near-natural lands → intensive rangelands.
Sub-Saharan BII: Intensity combined livestock density and nitrogen fertiliser inputs. Cattle, sheep and goat densities were summed and standardised within combinations of rainfall bands and soil-nutrient categories, recognising that environmental conditions influence the pressure associated with a given livestock density.
South African approach: SANLC can identify broad vegettaion groups, mapped erosion and previous cultivation, but cannot establish grazing pressure or ecological intactness from these classes alone. We are exploring livestock information alongside degradation and condition datasets, potentially including the SANBI nine-class condition layer. These sources will need to be evaluated for the pressures they represent in relation to the landscape contexts the experts were given, distinguishing current land-use intensity from persistent effects of historical degradation. Provisional low scores for natural cover should therefore not be interpreted as evidence of low pressure.
We could combine South Africa’s mapped livestock carrying capacity with global predictions of cattle, sheep and goat densities to estimate livestock pressure relative to the land’s capacity to support it. Animal densities would first be converted to compatible large-stock units (LSU), using appropriate species-specific factors. Carrying capacity expressed in hectares per LSU would be converted to LSU per hectare, allowing estimated livestock demand and capacity to be compared over the same grazing area.
This could provide a more locally relevant intensity proxy than livestock density alone. However, it would require checks on dataset dates, spatial resolution, supplementary feeding and the treatment of browsing animals and wildlife. The ratio would indicate potential land use pressure rather than demonstrate degradation, and would need evaluation against condition data and expert knowledge before being translated into the BII intensity gradient.

title: Segment land use and intensity allocation
text:
The aim of this section of the workflow is to assign each segment:

one dominant BII land use class; and
one land use intensity score between 0 and 1, where applicable.

The segment allocation has three steps:

calculate the proportion of each land use class in every segment;
assign one dominant land use class using a sequential decision tree;
calculate the segment intensity as the mean intensity of all valid pixels belonging to the chosen class

title: Segment land use and intensity allocation
Segment land use and intensity allocation
section: 2. Assign one BII land use class
text:
2. Assign one BII land use class
A candidate class becomes eligible for assignment when it covers more than 20% of the segment.
The classes are evaluated in the following priority order:

Settlements
Timber plantations
Tree croplands
Croplands
Protected lands
Untransformed lands

Where multiple classes exceed 20%, the class with the highest priority is assigned. Therefore the decision tree logic is:
IF settlement proportion > 0.20 assign Settlement
ELSE IF timber proportion > 0.20 assign Timber plantation
ELSE IF tree-crop proportion > 0.20 assign Tree cropland
ELSE IF cropland proportion > 0.20 assign Cropland
ELSE IF protected proportion > 0.20 assign Protected land
ELSE assign Untransformed land
Example, if:

settlement proportion = 0.25;
cropland proportion = 0.30; and
both exceed 0.20.

The segment is assigned to Settlements, because settlements have higher priority than croplands.

Examples








Segment composition
Assigned class
Reason




15% settlement, 30% cropland, 55% untransformed
Croplands
Settlement does not exceed 20%, but cropland does


22% timber, 35% cropland, 43% untransformed
Timber plantations
Both exceed 20%, but timber has higher priority


10% cropland, 25% protected, 65% untransformed
Protected lands
Protected cover exceeds 20% and no higher-priority class does


10% settlement, 10% crop, 15% protected, 65% untransformed
Untransformed lands
No other class exceeds 20%


25% settlement inside a protected area
Settlements
Transformed land is assigned before protected land



Note, a higher-priority transformed land use can override the protected assignment.
The allocation logic is implemented in reverse order in GEE because later where() statements overwrite earlier assignments. In other words, “where” the condition is true, replace the current value with the specified class.
var assignedLandUse = ee.Image(BII_UNTRANSFORMED)

  .where(
    propProtected.gt(0.20),
    BII_PROTECTED
  )

  .where(
    propCropland.gt(0.20),
    BII_CROPLAND
  )

  .where(
    propTreeCrop.gt(0.20),
    BII_TREE_CROP
  )

  .where(
    propTimber.gt(0.20),
    BII_TIMBER
  )

  .where(
    propSettlement.gt(0.20),
    BII_SETTLEMENT
  )

  .rename('bii_land_use');

title: Segment land use and intensity allocation
text:
3. Assign land use intensity
Land use class and land use intensity are separate attributes. For example, two segments may both be assigned to Settlements, but one may contain mainly smallholdings while the other contains industrial land. They therefore have the same broad land use class but different intensity scores.
The preliminary NLC intensity categories are converted to the following numeric scale:








Intensity category
Score
Interpretation




Low
0
Lowest mapped intensity within that broad land use class


Medium
0.5
Intermediate mapped intensity


High
1
Highest mapped intensity


Unknown
Not yet assigned
Requires an additional intensity layer or decision


n/a
Class-specific rule
No within-class gradient is currently used




Current class-level rules







BII land use
Current intensity treatment




Settlements
Mean of valid low, medium and high settlement-intensity pixels in the segment


Timber plantations
Fixed provisionally at 1


Tree croplands
Mean of valid tree-crop intensity pixels in the segment


Croplands
Mean of valid cropland intensity pixels in the segment


Protected lands
Fixed provisionally at 0; effectiveness may be assessed separately by biome


Untransformed lands
Assigned from available NLC indicators or additional biome-specific condition and pressure datasets





How the segment mean is calculated
Only pixels belonging to the assigned BII land use class are included in the intensity calculation.
For example, suppose a segment is assigned to Settlements and contains 20 valid settlement pixels:



Settlement intensity
Number of pixels
Contribution




Low, score 0
5
(5 = 0)


Medium, score 0.5
10
(10 = 5)


High, score 1
5
(5 = 5)



The segment intensity is:
\[
I_s = \frac{0 + 5 + 5}{20} = 0.5
\]
Cropland, protected and untransformed pixels occurring in the same segment are not included because the assigned class is Settlements.
More generally:
\[
I_s =
\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i I_i}
     {\sum_{i=1}^{n} a_i}
\]
where:

(I_s) is the intensity assigned to segment (s);
(I_i) is the intensity score of valid pixel (i);
(a_i) is the area of pixel (i); and
only pixels belonging to the assigned land use class are included.

title: Segment land use and intensity allocation
Segment land use and intensity allocation
text:
5. Untransformed intensity
In Progress
The NLC identifies whether land is broadly untransformed, but generally does not distinguish the intensity of use within natural vegetation, often used as rangelands. For this reason, most natural NLC classes are currently marked unknown. Additional information is required to distinguish land use intensity here. These intensity refinements will be added separately for each biome where suitable spatial data are available. For example, in Thicket, random-forest probabilities of intact, moderately degraded and severely degraded vegetation are being tested as a proxy for rangeland use intensity in segments assigned as Untransformed. Recent global products such as Livestock density at 1km resolution are being explored.

title: Segment land use and intensity allocation
text:
Output
The final spatial product is a two-band raster:
bii_land_use
bii_land_use_intensity

Band 1: bii_land_use
An integer value from 1 to 6 representing the dominant BII land use class assigned to each segment.


Band 2: bii_land_use_intensity
A continuous value from 0 to 1 representing land use intensity within the assigned class.
The two bands must be interpreted together. An intensity of 0 for a settlement and an intensity of 0 for an untransformed segment represent the low-intensity endpoints of two different land use classes.

title: Segment land use and intensity allocation
section: Segment vs. grid broad land cover composition
text:
Segment vs. grid broad land cover composition
We examined land cover composition in a northern Limpopo case study in a mixed use landscape to assess whether segments capture more coherent land use units than a regular 1 × 1 km grid. For each unit, we calculated the proportion of mapped terrestrial area occupied by each broad NLC category and applied the same >20% allocation thresholds and priority rules. Composition was then averaged within each assigned class, giving each unit equal weight.
Segments contained higher mean proportions of their assigned land cover (FIg. 1) than grid cells for settlements, timber plantations, tree croplands and croplands. Both approaches produced predominantly untransformed cover within Protected and Untransformed units. These preliminary results suggest that segments better separate broad land uses in this landscape.



Figure 1. Mean broad land cover composition of segments and 1 × 1 km grid cells by assigned BII land use class in the Limpopo case study. Colours represent underlying land cover; protected status is applied separately during allocation and therefore does not appear as a land-cover category.


The assigned land use class also matched the dominant underlying land cover more frequently in segments than in grid cells, particularly for croplands, tree croplands and settlements. This indicates that segment-based labels more often represent the largest land cover component within an assessment unit. The comparison measures agreement between allocation and mapped composition, rather than classification accuracy.



Figure 2. Percentage of segments and 1 × 1 km grid cells in which the assigned BII land use class matches the dominant underlying land cover in the Limpopo case study. Dominance denotes the largest share of mapped terrestrial area. Protected lands are excluded because protection is an overlapping management designation rather than a land cover category.
